plain: Gradient history is the record an optimizer keeps of the gradients it has seen recently, so that a step can depend on more than the latest batch.
ours: AdamW keeps two running records for every weight: an average of recent gradients (about the last 10 steps) and an average of their squares (about the last 1,000 steps). Muon keeps one record per matrix, the momentum, which at our setting of 0.9 covers about the last 10 steps.
deeper: A running average with factor beta remembers about 1/(1 - beta) steps: beta 0.9 is about 10, beta 0.999 is about 1,000. Two consequences for AdamW. After a sudden drop in gradient size, its squares-record still remembers the large gradients, so its steps shrink until the record catches up. Under pure noise, the average of the gradients partly cancels while the average of their squares does not, so its step falls to about sqrt((1 - beta)/(1 + beta)), which is 0.23 at beta 0.9. These are the textbook formulas applied to our settings; we have not logged them per matrix. Muon's step does not shrink in either case.

papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks

quiz.q: What does keeping a gradient history let an optimizer do?
options: Make a step depend on recent gradients, not only on the latest batch
quiz.why: The history smooths and reshapes steps using what was seen over the last few steps.

quiz.q: A running average uses factor 0.9. About how many recent steps does it effectively remember?
quiz.why: The memory is about 1/(1 - 0.9) = 10 steps. A factor of 0.999 would give about 1,000.

wrong.3: 1,000 steps belongs to a factor of 0.999, the usual setting for AdamW's squares-record.

quiz.q: Gradients suddenly become 100 times smaller. AdamW's squares-record has a memory of about 1,000 steps. What happens to AdamW's steps?
options: They shrink for a while, until the record catches up
They stop for the rest of training
quiz.why: The short average of gradients drops at once, but the long average of squares still remembers the big ones, so the ratio is small for roughly that long. Muon's step does not shrink.

wrong.0: That would be true if both records forgot at the same speed. The squares-record forgets slowly.

quiz.q: Why do AdamW's steps get smaller when gradients are pure noise, even if their size has not changed?
options: The learning rate is lowered automatically
The average of noisy gradients partly cancels, while the average of their squares does not
quiz.why: Random directions cancel when averaged, so the numerator shrinks, but squares are always positive and keep their size. At beta 0.9 the ratio falls to about 0.23.

wrong.3: AdamW does not detect noise; the shrinkage is a side effect of averaging.

plain: Momentum is a running average of recent gradients that the optimizer steps along, so one noisy batch cannot push the weights far in a wrong direction.
ours: Our optimizer uses a momentum of 0.9 by default, which averages over roughly the last 10 steps. At batch sizes of 1 to 16 it is what removes most of the noise. Muon takes the momentum of a whole matrix and evens out its directions (see orthogonal matrix) to make the step.
deeper: With factor beta = 0.9 the buffer averages about 10 steps. If the gradient is a steady signal plus independent noise, averaging raises the signal-to-noise ratio by about sqrt((1 + beta)/(1 - beta)) = 4.4 compared with one step. That figure assumes the signal stays the same over the window; if it drifts, 4.4 is an upper bound. The cost is lag: when the right direction changes, momentum keeps pushing the old way for about 10 steps. We have not measured an effect on generalisation.

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks

options: It averages recent gradients, so a step follows the trend and not one noisy batch
It makes the learning rate bigger over time
It stores the best weights seen so far
quiz.why: Momentum is a running average of recent gradients. Steps follow that average.

quiz.q: With momentum 0.9, one very large wrong gradient arrives once. How does its influence on later steps behave?
options: It fades gradually over roughly 10 to 20 steps
It affects only the next step
quiz.why: Each step multiplies the old buffer by 0.9, so the large gradient fades over about 10 to 20 steps.

wrong.0: That would be no momentum at all; the buffer keeps a decaying share of the old value.

quiz.q: Why does momentum matter more at batch 16 than at batch 256?
options: Small batches give noisier gradients, and averaging removes noise
Momentum only works at small batch sizes
quiz.why: A small batch is a small sample of the data, so its gradient is the true direction plus a lot of noise. Averaging over about 10 steps removes much of it.

quiz.q: At momentum 0.9, by about what factor does averaging improve the signal-to-noise ratio if the true gradient stays steady?
quiz.why: The factor is sqrt((1 + 0.9)/(1 - 0.9)) = 4.4. It is an upper bound if the signal drifts within the window.

wrong.3: 10 is the number of steps averaged. The signal-to-noise gain is its square-root-like factor, 4.4.

quiz.q: What is a cost of momentum?
options: It reacts late when the right direction changes
It increases the number of weights
quiz.why: The buffer remembers the old direction, so it lags for about 10 steps after a change.

plain: An orthogonal matrix turns or flips things without stretching any direction, so all of its directions are equally strong.
ours: Muon replaces the momentum matrix with an approximately orthogonal one before stepping. The gradient still decides which directions the matrix changes in, but every direction the method reaches gets a step of similar size, however faint the gradient was along it. 'Strong' means a lot of the gradient lies along that direction. In one of our heads, the momentum of an MLP matrix (1024 x 256) had a strongest direction about 10,000 times its weakest. After the update the strongest 100 or so directions sit between 0.7 and 1.2, and the weakest stay small.
deeper: For a gradient matrix G = U S V^T (S holds the strengths, called singular values), the nearest orthogonal matrix is U V^T: every strength is replaced by 1. Computing that exactly is expensive, so Muon runs five Newton-Schulz iterations, a fixed polynomial with coefficients (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315) chosen to put the strengths roughly between 0.7 and 1.3. The Muon post reports that this error does not hurt. Directions far weaker than the strongest are not pulled up within five steps. Textbook: the Muon post; ours: the same five iterations.

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks
Moonlight: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training

quiz.q: What is special about an orthogonal matrix's directions?
options: They all point the same way
quiz.why: An orthogonal matrix does not stretch any direction: all strengths are 1.

quiz.q: Why does Muon orthogonalise its update?
options: So every direction gets a step of similar size, not just those with the largest gradient
quiz.why: Without it the biggest gradient directions dominate. Orthogonalising gives faint directions a real step too.

quiz.q: Muon uses five Newton-Schulz iterations rather than computing the exact orthogonal matrix. Why?
options: It is cheaper to run, and an approximate result does not hurt
Five is the number of layers
The exact result needs the data
It is required by the GPU
quiz.why: The exact decomposition is expensive on GPUs; a few matrix multiplications give a close-enough answer (the Muon post reports no harm).

quiz.q: After five iterations, how orthogonal is the result in practice?
options: Roughly: the strengths land between about 0.7 and 1.3
Only the weakest direction is fixed
Only the strongest direction is fixed
quiz.why: The coefficients trade exactness for speed, leaving the strengths between about 0.7 and 1.3.

quiz.q: A momentum matrix has a strongest direction 10,000 times its weakest. After five iterations, what happens to the weakest direction?
options: It becomes as strong as the strongest
It stays small, because five steps cannot lift something that faint
quiz.why: The iteration lifts moderately weak directions toward 1, but directions far weaker than the strongest remain small within five steps.

wrong.0: That is the ideal exact result; with five iterations it does not reach the faintest directions.
